name: Cabbage
summary: How Filipino farmers usually grow repolyo from seedlings raised in a seedbed and set out on beds or ridges, in the highlands all year and in the lowlands in the cool months. For small farms that want the usual routine first, then the changes that bring firmer, cleaner heads.
season: In the highlands, such as Benguet, Mountain Province and the Bukidnon uplands, cabbage is grown in most months, with extra care in the heavy rain months. In the lowlands it is grown only in the cooler months, usually with seed sown around September to November and heads cut by February, using varieties that take some heat.
material: Seed, about 200 to 250 g a hectare, sown in a seedbed or seed boxes. Seedlings are pricked out, fed lightly, hardened, and transplanted at about 25 to 35 days old, when they are short and sturdy.
spacing: Lowland ridges about 50 cm apart with plants 40 cm apart. On raised beds two rows 50 by 40 cm. Highland growers on beds often plant 30 to 35 cm each way for smaller heads. One seedling a hill.
water: Watered right after transplanting, then by furrow or sprinkler about every 8 to 12 days in dry weather, depending on the soil. Young plants need steady moisture. Once heads form farmers water less so the heads do not split or rot.
fertilizer: Cabbage is a heavy feeder. Highland farmers are known for heavy use of chicken dung on the beds, about 2 to 3 tons a hectare or more, plus complete fertilizer and urea. A common lowland guide is 3 bags of 14 14 14 a hectare three to five days after transplanting and 3 bags of urea at about 30 days.
care: Hand weeding and shallow cultivation from two to three weeks after transplanting until the plants are half grown, rice straw or plastic mulch, light hilling up with the side dressing, and frequent checks for diamondback moth and cabbage head borers.
harvest: Lowland varieties are usually ready about 55 to 60 days after transplanting and many highland varieties at about 60 to 75 days, when the heads are firm. Heads are cut with a knife with some wrapper leaves left on, sorted, and packed in sacks or crates. Heads left too long, or pushed by too much water and fertilizer, split.

ways.label: Seedbed then transplant (punla at lipat tanim)

steps.title: Make the seedbed and sow
steps.how: Prepare a bed about 1 m by 10 m in full sun near water, or seed boxes with garden soil, rotted manure, sand and rice hull ash. Clean the soil by burning rice straw on top or pouring boiling water, then sow in shallow lines about 5 cm apart and cover lightly.
steps.tip: Highland growers often put a plastic roof over the seedbeds against hard rain.

parts.title: Pick a sunny, level spot
parts.how: Set the seedbed on level ground in full sun and close to water. A bed about 1 m wide and 10 m long is the usual size. For a small planting, use wooden seed boxes instead.

parts.title: Mix the seed box soil
parts.how: For boxes, take two parts each of garden soil, well rotted manure and rice hull ash, add one part each of sand and compost, and mix well. The mix stays loose, so the roots come out whole at pricking time.

parts.title: Clean the soil
parts.how: Pour boiling water over the bed or the box mix and cover it with plastic until it cools, or spread dry rice straw over the bed and burn it. This kills the fungus that makes seedlings fall over at the base.

parts.title: Water, then sow in lines
parts.how: Water the bed or box before sowing. Draw shallow lines across it about 5 cm apart, drop the seed thinly along each line and cover it lightly with fine soil.
parts.tip: About 200 to 250 grams of seed raises enough seedlings for one hectare.

parts.title: Soak it for the first days
parts.how: Keep the bed fully wet for the first three days, then water less once the seedlings are up so the soil does not stay soggy.

parts.title: Roof it against hard rain
parts.how: In the highlands and in the rainy months, set a simple plastic roof over the bed so heavy rain does not beat the seedlings down or wash the seed out.

steps.title: Prick out the seedlings
steps.how: About a week after the seedlings come up, move the sturdy, healthy ones to another bed or box about 5 by 5 cm apart.

parts.title: Ready a second bed or box
parts.how: Fill another box or prepare another small bed with the same clean soil mix, and water it well before you start.

parts.title: Choose the sturdy ones
parts.how: About a week after the seedlings come up, pick only the short, sturdy, healthy ones. Leave behind the thin, pale or spotted seedlings.
parts.time: about a week after they come up

parts.title: Lift and reset them
parts.how: Lift each seedling with a little soil on its roots, holding it by a leaf and not by the stem. Set them about 5 by 5 cm apart in the new bed and firm the soil around each one.

parts.title: Water and shade
parts.how: Water them gently right after moving and keep them out of the hottest sun until they stand up again.

steps.title: Plow and harrow
steps.how: Clear the old crop and weeds, then plow and harrow two to three times about a week apart.

steps.title: Feed the seedlings
steps.how: One week after pricking, water the seedlings with a weak mix of complete fertilizer in water, then sprinkle plain water so the leaves do not burn.

steps.title: Harden the seedlings
steps.how: In the last week, water the seedlings only when they start to wilt so they toughen up before transplanting.

steps.title: Form ridges or beds and add manure
steps.how: Make ridges about 50 cm apart in the lowlands, or raised beds about 1 m wide where drainage is poor and in the highlands. Mix chicken dung or other manure into the soil.

steps.title: Transplant late in the afternoon
steps.how: Set one hardened seedling a hill on moist soil, with the growing tip above the soil. On ridges plant 40 cm apart. On beds use two rows 50 by 40 cm, or about 30 to 35 cm each way for small heads. Water right away.
steps.tip: Shade newly set plants with pieces of banana stalk or leaves for a few days.

parts.title: Pick the right seedlings
parts.how: Use hardened seedlings about 25 to 35 days old that are short and stocky, with a good ball of roots. Tall, soft seedlings break and wilt in the field.

parts.title: Plant on moist soil in the late afternoon
parts.how: Plant when the soil is moist and the sun is low, so the seedlings have the cool night to settle. Set them at the same depth they grew in the seedbed, with the growing tip above the soil.

parts.title: Firm the soil and water
parts.how: Press the soil firmly around the roots so no air pockets are left, then water each plant right away.

parts.title: Cover them for a few days
parts.how: Shade each new plant with a piece of banana stalk, a few leaves or a twig with leaves until it stops wilting at midday.

steps.title: First fertilizer
steps.how: Three to five days after transplanting, put complete fertilizer (14 14 14) a little away from the plants and cover it.

steps.title: Replace dead seedlings
steps.how: Fill gaps with spare seedlings from the seedbed in the first week.

steps.title: Scout for worms and moths
steps.how: Check under the leaves for the small green larvae of the diamondback moth, webbed larvae at the growing tip, cutworms and aphids. Crush egg masses by hand.

steps.title: Cultivate, weed and mulch
steps.how: Loosen the soil and pull weeds two to three weeks after transplanting. Rice straw laid between plants keeps weeds down and the soil moist.

steps.title: Side dress urea
steps.how: About a month after transplanting, put urea 6 to 8 cm from the base of each plant and cover it with soil.

steps.title: Water by furrow as needed
steps.how: Water through the furrows every week or so in dry weather, then water less once the heads start to form so they do not crack or rot.

steps.title: Cut the firm heads
steps.how: When the heads feel hard and compact, cut them with a sharp knife, leaving a few wrapper leaves to protect the head.

steps.title: Sort and pack
steps.how: Throw rotten heads into the compost pit, dab the cut base with lime water against rot, and pack the heads in sacks or crates kept in the shade.

mistakes: Transplanting old, leggy seedlings that were never hardened, so many die or head poorly.
Planting in the hot lowland months with a variety meant for the cool highlands.
Heavy watering once the heads form, which makes them crack and rot.
Spraying on a fixed calendar, which kills the small wasps that keep diamondback moth down.
Growing cabbage after cabbage family crops on the same beds year after year, so club root and soil pests build up.
Leaving firm heads in the field too long until they split.
better: Choose a variety for your elevation and season, with heat tolerance for lowland planting.
Test the soil, lime acid soils and fertilize by the result instead of piling on dung and urea.
Raise clean, hardened seedlings in a covered seedbed or trays.
Scout twice a week and act only when worm counts climb, so natural enemies survive.
Rotate with crops outside the cabbage family and plow under old crop debris after harvest.
Harvest at the firm head stage and keep the heads shaded on the way to market.
